title: Interfaces, error handling and contracts

objectives.text: Specify C++ input/output units, bounds, ownership/lifetimes and mutation guarantees, then implement checked nonnegative cents accumulation before arithmetic.
Distinguish typed domain failure, valid zero and throwing boundary policy without erasing failure as success or claiming external atomic rollback.
Distinguish basic, strong and nothrow guarantees and test failure paths before and after a bounded commit.
Choose owning versus borrowed vocabulary types, distinguish absence from failure, and implement a C++20 typed fallback for C++23 expected.

blocks.markdown: An interface contract names units, representation/range, ownership, lifetime, side effects and failure semantics. Here input is a valid live contiguous sequence of at most 1000 long long nonnegative integer cents, result is exact cents if representable, and no input or external state is modified. A span carries a pointer/extent view, not ownership or authentication. The caller must supply valid storage for the whole call, with no concurrent mutation. The helper does not parse arbitrary bytes, verify account identity or convert currencies.

std::span<const long long> is a C++20 nonowning view that lets arrays/vectors expose a contiguous sequence without copying their elements. const applies to access through the view; another alias could still change storage unless the caller prevents it. The helper consumes the view synchronously and does not store/return it. Constructing a span from an invalid pointer/extent cannot be repaired by checking values later. C++20 span operator[] has a bounds precondition, not a guaranteed checked-at facility; this example uses a range loop over a valid span.

A std::variant<long long,SumError> represents either one value or one declared error here. SumError separates too-many, negative and arithmetic-overflow conditions. A present zero is a legitimate success, not an absent/error sentinel. General variant types can be valueless_by_exception under some throwing operations; this helper directly constructs alternatives of scalar types and does not mutate a throwing alternative. Do not promote this narrow design into a claim that every variant can never be valueless. Callers inspect the alternative instead of assuming a value. Error precedence is size first, then the first negative/range failure encountered in sequence order; the helper does not continue after an error to collect every later issue.

blocks.title: Preserve the range invariant before adding

steps.text: Initialize total=0, satisfying 0<=total<=M. For each amount value, reject value<0 first.
Since total<=M, M-total is safely representable and nonnegative. If value>M-total, reject before evaluating total+value. Otherwise the new total remains between 0 and M.

For [M,1], the first value reaches M; the second fails 1>M-M=0 without evaluating M+1. For an empty input the result is present 0. The helper returns no partial total as successful output after a later error.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: 6, 0, negative, overflow. The valid input and error cases are kept distinct; range validation happens before addition. The view and its input arrays stay alive for each call. Local computation publishes a typed result and does not modify the arrays, but it does not prove crash-safe persistent transactions or validate the construction of an arbitrary incoming span.

blocks.markdown: Use a typed result when ordinary input/domain failure is part of the expected interface, and choose how callers must handle each case. Exceptions can express a failure that the current call cannot fulfill when the surrounding codebase uses that policy. There is no universal rule that one mechanism is always faster/safer. Do not return 0 for every failure, log-and-continue as though success, catch(...) and discard the cause, or mark a potentially throwing wrapper noexcept merely to suppress concerns. noexcept is a promise whose violation terminates, not an automatic error handler.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: 0, input rejected, range rejected. This complete independent program wraps the SAME checked computation with a documented exception policy. It catches the specific expected categories at the demonstrated boundary. A valid zero stays successful; bad input is not silently changed to zero. The throwing adapter is not declared noexcept and does not mutate external state.

blocks.markdown: A read-only local computation can leave caller data unchanged on a returned error or thrown adapter failure. That is a scoped no-mutation result, not proof that a later file/database/order call is atomically rolled back. A production interface also needs source binding, parsing, protocol version, cancellation/timeouts, resource limits and recovery evidence. When providing a durable service, define commit points and retriable versus permanent failures separately from C++ exception syntax.

Independent transfer: exercise the declared too-many policy for more than 1000 amounts and test it without touching the input. Verify empty input, zero amounts, negative at the first/last position, M alone, [M,0] and [M,1]. Check typed result and throwing adapter agree on every supported case, preserve original arrays and never convert a failure into successful zero. Explain what the span caller must guarantee that this helper cannot check.

Sources: [span](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span.html), [variant alternatives/valueless state](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/variant.html), and [Core Guidelines interface/ownership/error guidance](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines.html). C++20 is fixed; later library facilities such as std::expected or span::at are not silently assumed available.

Failure has a state contract, not only a return channel

An operation can throw and still protect state. The basic exception guarantee means invariants remain true and resources are not leaked, although values may change. The strong guarantee means a failed operation has no observable effect within its declared state boundary. The nothrow guarantee means no exception escapes; nofail is stronger operational language meaning the promised operation succeeds, rather than merely returning an error. These are not synonyms for fast, durable, thread-safe or recoverable. A function with no guarantee can leave invalid state. State the boundary: an in-memory ledger and an external order gateway are different participants.

Read the injected failure trace

Ledger.cents is always between 0 and 100 in this bounded example. Starting from 37, basic(true) sets it to 0 and throws: the invariant survives but rollback does not, so this is basic, not strong. strong(true) prepares a scalar candidate and throws before assignment, leaving 37. On success both set 20. The assignment is nonthrowing for int. There are no hidden callbacks or externally visible effects. This proves a scoped strong guarantee by construction; it does not undo a log write, network send or mutation of another object performed before the throw.

Prepare first, commit only with a nonthrowing final action

A general transactional update first validates, then builds a candidate without modifying the live object, then commits using an operation known not to throw under its allocator/type conditions. Copy-and-swap is one possible implementation, not a magic property of every swap. Copying can allocate and fail. If commit itself can throw after partially changing the destination, the strong guarantee has not been established. Test failure injection at every potentially throwing preparation stage. Avoid tests that only exercise success and infer rollback. An exception test should compare full protected state and resource counts against a before snapshot.

Unwinding and noexcept are separate mechanisms

The Guard destructor runs when the exception unwinds its enclosing scope, returning the live count to zero. Catch exceptions by const reference when only inspecting them, so derived information is not sliced by a copied base. Catch only where a defined recovery/translation can be made. Destructors used during unwinding must not throw another exception. noexcept specifies that an escaping exception calls terminate; it is not a try/catch, a proof of no failure or a request for automatic rollback. The reset body here is actually nonthrowing because it only assigns a representable scalar. Do not mark arbitrary allocation/I/O code noexcept to make it look safer.

Choose a channel with latency evidence

Exceptions, typed results and error codes express different API policies. Throwing involves runtime-dependent unwinding and often allocation or metadata costs; latency-sensitive hot paths may forbid it to bound recovery behavior. That does not prove a typed-result implementation is always faster, or that a nonthrowing function meets a deadline. Measure normal and failing paths separately with representative distributions, optimization flags and tail latency. A benchmark that never throws cannot estimate exception recovery time. No universal timing ratio is claimed here.

blocks.markdown:
Guided transfer: replace the scalar candidate with a two-field quantity/notional state. Define both fields' invariant, inject a failure after each preparation step, and compare every live field before/after failure. Hints: (1) compute into locals, (2) do not write the first live field before validating the second, (3) keep the final commit nonthrowing. Solution outline: validate both input ranges, prepare both representable integers, then assign the scalar pair only after all possible exceptions. This is one-thread local state, not atomic observation by another thread.

Independent transfer: write a bounded vector update that offers the strong guarantee without assuming vector element operations or allocators are harmless. State copy/allocation/swap conditions, add injected preparation failure, success and unchanged-state tests, and show one implementation that offers only basic safety. Hints: (1) build a separate candidate, (2) justify your exact commit operation and allocator conditions, (3) track all externally visible side effects. Review rubric: sound invariant, failure at each stage, no leaked resource, precise guarantee boundary. No automatic code-submission pass is claimed by the concept questions.

References: [exception safety guarantees and unwinding](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/exceptions), [noexcept boundary and termination](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/noexcept_spec), [destruction during unwinding](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/destructor), and [Core Guidelines error-handling and invariants](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines.html). These sources establish language mechanisms and design guidance. The scalar ledger invariant, failure injection points and scoped commit proof are authored examples, not durable transaction guarantees.

Choose what the interface means before choosing syntax

std::span<T> is a C++20 nonowning contiguous sequence view, carrying extent without extending storage lifetime. std::string_view (C++17) is a nonowning character view, not necessarily null-terminated. Neither makes referenced storage immutable through other aliases or safe against concurrent modification. std::optional<T> (C++17) means value or absence with no built-in reason; a present zero is still a value. std::expected<T,E> is C++23 value-or-error with a distinguished error type, not part of the C++20 baseline. A domain where absence is normal may suit optional; malformed input needing a reason suits a result with a typed error.

A complete borrowed parse boundary

parse_cents synchronously consumes a string_view without storing it. It accepts an optional leading plus, then one or more decimal digits representing a nonnegative int. It rejects whitespace, minus, trailing characters, empty input and a lone plus. from_chars uses the view end pointer and does not require a zero terminator. The first-digit check rejects negative signs before conversion; a successful parse must consume the entire view. from_chars reports integer overflow as result_out_of_range. The fixtures explicitly require int to represent 2147483647, checked at compile time rather than assumed universally. The string backing the view must remain valid for the call.

std::error_code has a category as well as a number

An error_code carries an integer and an error_category. Equal numeric values from unrelated categories need not mean the same thing. std::make_error_code(std::errc::invalid_argument) constructs the portable generic-category representation; compare with std::errc conditions when asking the portable meaning instead of comparing raw platform integers or English message text. Our ParseError wraps this code, so callers can retain a typed parse-error boundary. Zero-valued error codes conventionally mean success, but this API stores only a failure inside ParseError and uses the result alternative to distinguish success, including parsed zero. It never returns a default value while silently dropping an error.

C++23 expected and the C++20 fallback are not interchangeable libraries

With __cpp_lib_expected >= 202202L, Result is expected<int,ParseError>; return int for success and unexpected(ParseError{...}) for failure. has_value checks before value access; error() is only used on the error branch. value() can throw bad_expected_access on failure. Dereferencing a failed result does not provide the checked value() behavior. C++23 monadic operations such as and_then require their own later feature macro value, 202211L; they are not used here. A C++23 compiler mode alone does not prove the standard library provides expected.

Fallback semantics and measured availability

Without that feature macro the complete program uses variant<int,ParseError> with explicit success/error access helpers. This is a narrow C++20 fallback, not a backported implementation of all expected operations, layout or exception guarantees. General variant can become valueless_by_exception; the chosen alternatives and construction paths here do not exercise throwing alternative replacement. Do not hide the distinction behind an unqualified claim that expected ran. The local C++20 output must say native_expected=0; a supported C++23 run must say 1. Both should return identical parse outcomes on the same corpus. The earlier span lesson and string_view lifetime lesson remain prerequisites in learning order, not evidence that every borrowed API is safe.

Optional absence is not parse failure

first_positive takes a valid span synchronously and returns a copied int in optional. Empty input or no positive element yields nullopt, not a malformed-message error. Returning optional<int> avoids returning a dangling reference into the span, but does not validate an invalid span supplied by a caller. Test zero distinctly from absence, successful boundary values, exact end consumption and oversized digit strings. Error precedence matters: this implementation checks the initial digit before conversion, then reports conversion range errors before trailing-data errors. These policies are part of the API, not universal parsing rules.

blocks.markdown:
Guided transfer: parse the view "12x" and explain why a successful prefix conversion is not success for this whole-field API. Hints: (1) inspect from_chars.ptr, (2) compare it with the end of the view, (3) return invalid_argument if trailing data remains. Solution: reject because the pointer stops at x, even though the numeric prefix fits.

Independent transfer: implement a quantity field bounded to 0..1000 with distinct syntax, range and business-limit errors. Keep backing storage alive, test leading plus, zero, 1000, 1001, very long digits and trailing characters. Hints: (1) define error precedence first, (2) do not confuse missing optional field with present malformed field, (3) run identical outcome checks under fallback and native expected. Review rubric: ownership/lifetime contract, full consumption, separate error reason, no unchecked failed access. The native branch is a separate toolchain gate, not established by a fallback pass.

References: [span lifetime and extent](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/container/span), [string_view ownership and lifetime](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/string/basic_string_view), [optional presence](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/utility/optional), [from_chars parsing and result pointer](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/utility/from_chars), [error_code category semantics](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/error/error_code.html), [expected and its feature macro](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/utility/expected), [library feature-test macros](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/utility/feature_test), and [variant fallback access](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/utility/variant). The exact parse grammar, error precedence and chosen fallback wrapper are authored contracts. Native C++23 availability and local execution are reported separately from these mechanism references.

summary: A checked interface states units/range/ownership/lifetime and preserves failure as failure. A typed result and a throwing adapter can share one guarded computation; valid zero, local no-mutation behavior and durable external atomicity are different claims.
